Problem: What kind of guarantee black-box evals can provide about model capabilities.
Write-up text before the decision: r design & coverage of black box evaluations). As a non-example, possessing the kind of foundational scientific understanding which would allow someone to confidently say "We have run this evaluation suite and we now know once and for all that this system is definitely not capable of x, regardless of whatever elicitation techniques are developed in the future" seems me to be Science-of-AI-complete and is thus a non-starter for a north star for an agenda aimed at developing stronger inability arguments. When I fast forward the development of black box evals aimed at supporting inability arguments, I see us arriving at a place where we have: 1. More SWE-Benchesque evaluations across critical domains which are perhaps "more Verified" by having higher quality expert judgement passed upon them. 2. Some kind of library which brings together a family of different SOTA prompting and finetuning recipes to apply to any evaluation scenario. 3. More data points and stronger [forecasts for post training enhancements](https:/ HIS COMMENT: These are all good points. I think there are two types of forecasts we could make with evals: 1\. strict guarantees: almost like mathematical predictions where we can proof that the model is not going to behave in a specific way even with future elicitation techniques. 2\. probabilistic predictions: We predict a distribution of capabilities or a range and agree on a threshold that should not be crossed. For example, if the 95% upper bound of that distribution crosses our specified capability level, we treat the model differently.
Previous context: A research team is developing black-box evaluations intended to support arguments that a model lacks a dangerous capability. === key 792f71e12a14
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: Whether the argument that AGI will scheme is trivially compelling.
Write-up text before the decision: it seems strange to me. And yet there are intelligent and well-informed people who say things like "there's no empirical evidence for scheming in AIs" in all seriousness. So I'd like to understand that perspective better. While I don't fully understand the perspective that needs to be convinced that scheming is likely, I do have some guesses. I think on the whole it stems from understanding current AI systems well, and reasoning from there. Current systems do not really scheme; they lack the capacity. Those who reason by analogy with humans or with fictional or hypothetical generally superintelligent AI see scheming as extremely likely from a misaligned AGI, because they're assuming it will have all the necessary cognitive capacities. There are more nuanced views, but I think those are the two starting points that generate this dramatic difference in opinions. Some more specific common cruxes of disagreement on scheming likelihood: * Will AGI have consequentialist goals HIS COMMENT: I think it's actually not that trivial. 1\. The AI has goals, but presumably, we give it decently good goals when we start. So, there is a real question of why these goals end up changing from aligned to misaligned. I think outcome-based RL and instrumental convergence are an important part of the answer. If the AI kept the goals we originally gave it with all side constraints, I think the chances of scheming would be much lower. 2\. I guess we train the AI to follow some side constraints, e.g., to be helpful, harmless, and honest, which should reduce the probability of scheming.
Previous context: A researcher is trying to understand why some intelligent, well-informed people seriously claim there is no empirical evidence that future AI systems will scheme, while others reason by analogy to humans or hypothetical superintelligences and treat scheming by a misaligned advanced system as nearly certain. A common argument is that a misaligned AGI would trivially be expected to scheme. But the researcher notes the system would presumably start with reasonably good goals, raising the question of why those goals would shift, and that training toward helpful, harmless, and honest behavior might act as a side constraint lowering scheming probability.
Previous question: How should the team assess whether the argument that an advanced AI will scheme is trivially compelling?

I agree that it's not that simple in practice, because we'd try to avoid that by giving side constraints; but it is that simple in the abstract, and by default. If it followed our initial goal *as we intended it* there would be no problem; but the core of much alignment worry is that it's really hard to get exactly what we intended into an AI as its goal. I also agree that good HHH training might be enough to overcome the consequentialist/instrumental logic of scheming. Those tendencies would function as side constraints. Which would win out would be a result of exactly how that goal was implemented in the AIs decision-making procedures, particularly the ones surrounding learning. HIS COMMENT: Good point. That's another crux for which RL seems relevant. From the perspective of 10 years ago, specifying any goal into the AI seemed incredibly hard since we expected it would have to go through utility functions. With LLMs, this completely changed. Now it's almost trivial to give the goal, and it probably even has a decent understanding of the side constraints by default.
Previous context: A research team is discussing what story best explains why an advanced AI might scheme. One view holds that the core difficulty is that it is very hard to get exactly the intended goal into an AI, so even a system that faithfully follows its given goal may end up misaligned; another notes that with modern language models, specifying a goal and even conveying side constraints has become nearly trivial compared to older expectations that goals would have to be encoded through utility functions.
Previous question: How should the team weigh goal misgeneralization against other explanations as the main route to scheming risk?
